w: Built in 1851 by marine architect Asa Tift, this French Colonial house at 907 Whitehead Street was Hemingway's home from 1931 to 1939, where he wrote Green Hills of Africa and To Have and Have Not. Auctioned after his divorce, it became a museum in 1964, now home to dozens of polydactyl cats.
s: Hemingway's home, 1931-1939, and its six-toed cats
_facts: Built 1851 by Asa Tift in French Colonial style
Hemingway lived here 1931-1939 with wife Pauline Pfeiffer
Wrote Green Hills of Africa and To Have and Have Not here
Became a museum in 1964; National Historic Landmark in 1968

n: Harry S. Truman Little White House
w: President Harry Truman spent 175 days here across 11 visits, using this house in the Truman Annex as his winter White House. Unlike most presidential retreats it survives largely intact, a preserved slice of Cold War-era executive life tucked into Key West's Old Town.
s: Truman's winter White House, 175 days over 11 visits
_facts: Winter White House for President Harry S. Truman
Used during 11 visits totaling 175 days
Located in the Truman Annex neighborhood of Old Town

w: A painted concrete buoy at South and Whitehead Streets claims to mark the southernmost point in the continental US, though it is neither the true southernmost point of the mainland nor of Key West. The city installed it in 1983 to replace a small sign; a duplicate went up on Duval Street in 2025 during seawall repairs.
s: A concrete buoy claiming a title it doesn't quite hold
_facts: Installed by the city in 1983, replacing a small sign
Not actually the southernmost point of the mainland US or of Key West
Repainted after Hurricane Irma damage in 2017
A duplicate buoy was installed on Duval Street in 2025 during repairs

w: A historic bar on the corner of Greene and Duval since 1937, and one of Ernest Hemingway's regular haunts. It now hosts the annual Hemingway Days celebration, culminating in the Hemingway Look-Alike Contest, drawing bearded contestants chasing a resemblance to the writer who once drank here.
s: Hemingway's old bar, now home to the Look-Alike Contest
_facts: Open at the corner of Greene and Duval Streets since 1937
A frequent haunt of Ernest Hemingway
Hosts the annual Hemingway Days and Look-Alike Contest

w: Named for Florida's first territorial governor, William Pope Duval, this 1.25-mile spine of Key West runs coast to coast, lined with Bahamian and Victorian mansions preserved since the 1960s. Cuban immigrants arriving from the 1860s brought a cigar-rolling trade that once earned the city the nickname Cigar City USA.
s: Key West's mile-long spine, once Cigar City USA
_facts: Runs 1.25 miles from the Gulf of Mexico to the Atlantic
Named for Florida's first territorial governor, William Pope Duval
Cuban immigration from the 1860s brought a cigar-making trade
Designated a 'Great Street' by the American Planning Association in 2012

n: Basilica of St. Mary Star of the Sea
w: The oldest Catholic parish in the Archdiocese of Miami and one of the oldest in Florida, this minor basilica anchors Key West's Old Town. It stands as a contributing building within the Key West Historic District on the National Register of Historic Places, a quiet counterweight to the Duval Street bustle nearby.
s: Florida's oldest Catholic parish, raised to a basilica
_facts: Oldest parish in the Archdiocese of Miami
One of the oldest Catholic parishes in Florida
A minor basilica, contributing to the Key West Historic District

w: Standing across the street from the Hemingway House, the first Key West lighthouse was a 65-foot tower completed in 1825, lit by 15 lamps set in 15-inch reflectors to guide ships past the reef-strewn Florida Straits and into the harbor below.
s: A 65-foot beacon watching the reef since 1825
_facts: First tower completed in 1825, standing 65 feet tall
Originally lit by 15 lamps in 15-inch reflectors
Stands opposite the Ernest Hemingway House

w: A Victorian mansion built in 1896 in the Upper Duval district, steps from the southernmost point marker. Five US presidents have stayed within its walls over the years, and it now operates as a bed and breakfast facing the Atlantic surf.
s: An 1896 mansion that has hosted five US presidents
_facts: Built in 1896 as a Victorian mansion
Five US presidents have stayed there
Located in the Upper Duval district
Now operates as a bed and breakfast

w: Founded by treasure hunter Mel Fisher, this Greene Street museum holds artifacts salvaged from 17th-century wrecks including the Nuestra Senora de Atocha and Santa Margarita. A working conservation lab lets visitors watch pieces being restored, plus a gallery on Cuban balseros who fled by raft.
s: Treasure hunter Mel Fisher's shipwreck-artifact museum
_facts: Holds artifacts from the Atocha and Santa Margarita wrecks
Founded by Mel Fisher as a non-profit museum
Includes a working conservation and archaeology lab
Rotating gallery on Cuban rafters (balseros)

w: Berthed at Key West Bight, this schooner is the last surviving authentic working tall ship built in Florida. Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1984, she has served as flagship for both the state of Florida and the city of Key West itself.
s: The last authentic tall ship built in Florida
_facts: Last surviving authentic working tall ship built in Florida
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1984
Official flagship of Florida and of the city of Key West
Berthed at 202 William Street, Key West Bight

w: In 1860 the US Navy intercepted three illegal slave ships carrying 1,432 rescued Africans, held in quarantine at Key West. Some 294 died and were buried here. The graves lay forgotten until ground-penetrating radar located them in 2002, and the site joined the National Register of Historic Places a decade later.
s: Graves of 294 Africans rescued from slave ships in 1860
_facts: 294 rescued Africans died and were buried here in 1860
Discovered using ground-penetrating radar in 2002
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2012

w: Built in 1901 for the Florida State Troops after the volunteer Key West Rifles lost their gear in the 1886 fire, this armory later became the first home of the Studios of Key West artist community in 2006. Twelve artist studios still occupy the upper floor, while its main hall now hosts local theater rehearsals.
_facts: Built in 1901 for the Florida State Troops
Predecessor militia, the Key West Rifles, lost its gear in the 1886 fire
Became home to the Studios of Key West artist community in 2006

n: Martello Gallery-Key West Art and Historical Museum
w: Also known as the East Martello Tower, this fortification is the best-preserved example of Martello-style military architecture in the country. Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1972, it now houses a gallery of the Key West Art and Historical Museum inside its thick coral-stone walls.
_facts: Best-preserved example of Martello-style military architecture in the US
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1972
Located at 3501 South Roosevelt Boulevard

w: Housed in a recreation of a wrecker's warehouse built by Asa Tift, this museum uses actors and artifacts to tell 400 years of Keys shipwreck salvage. Many pieces come from the 1985 find of the Isaac Allerton, whose 1856 wreck brought the era's largest salvage award. Visitors can climb the 65-foot lookout tower.
s: A wrecker's warehouse turned shipwreck-salvage museum
_facts: Recreates the warehouse of wrecker tycoon Asa Tift
Features artifacts from the 1856 wreck of the Isaac Allerton
The Allerton salvage won the largest federal wrecking-court award for one vessel
Visitors can climb a 65-foot lookout tower
